speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OP SELECT STANDING COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER ACCOUNTS AND ESTIMATES
speechtext:
That standing order 63 of the House of Commons, relating to the appointment of select standing committees of the house be amended by adding to the select standing committees of the house for the present session a select standing committee on railways and shipping, owned, operated and controlled by the government to which will be referred the accounts and the estimates of the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Government Merchant Marine for the present session, for consideration and report to the house; provided however, that nothing in the resolution shall be construed to curtail in any way the full right of discussion in committee of supply, and that said committee consist of: Messrs. Beaubien, Beaubier, Bell (St. Antoine), Bothwell, Cantley, Chaplin, Duff, Euler, Fiset, Fraser (Cariboo), Geary, Gray, Gobeil, Hanbury, Heaps, Kennedy (Peace River), McGibbon, MacMillan (Saskatoon), Manion, Power, Price, and Stewart (Lethbridge).
I beg to say that this is in the same form as the motions previously moved in this respect.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OP SELECT STANDING COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER ACCOUNTS AND ESTIMATES
speechtext:
Before the motion is put to the house; in view of the guarantee of the credit of the Canadian Pacific Railway given by the government, and particularly in view of the statement issued in connection with the request for similar guarantees by the government of British Columbia, I wish to move this amendment:
That the first paragraph of the motion before the house be amended to read as follows:
That standing order 63 of the House of Commons relating to the appointment of the select standing committees of the house be amended by adding to the select standing committees of the house for the present session, a select standing committee on railways and shipping, owned, operated and controlled by the government, or whose borrowings have been guaranteed by the government, to which will be referred the accounts and the estimates of the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Government Merchant Marine for the present session, together with the accounts and estimates of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and their subsidiary companies, for consideration and report to the house.
In speaking before the annual meeting of shareholders of the Canadian Pacific Railway at Montreal during the present week, Mr. Beatty, the president of that company, stressed the seriousness of the railway situ-

Railways and Shipping
ation, we will assume with particular reference to his own company. He spoke of the necessity for a greater degree of unification of services and operation. He has indeed painted a very dark picture of the future outlook for the railways of Canada.
Therefore I believe that the affairs of the Canadian Pacific Railway should be investigated by this house, based on our guarantee of their securities. In support of that view I wish to quote what this government have said to the province of British Columbia- quite properly I think-that if the government of the province of British Columbia are to come to this government and ask for financial relief, this government should have the opportunity of reviewing their estimates. In order that the members of this house may get the full picture I consider it advisable to read the whole letter addressed by the Prime Minister of Canada to Mr. Pattullo, the premier of British Columbia, although perhaps it is not all germane to the point under discussion:
Ottawa, May 2, 1934.
Dear Mr. Pattullo,
Your request for financial assistance has been given the most careful consideration by council, and in reviewing your position we have had before us the letter of the Hon. John Hart, addressed to the Minister of Finance on February 26, which we have considered in the light of the letter addressed to Mr. Hart by the Minister of Finance on March 29, as well as the telegrams which have been exchanged between us on the same subject.
Notwithstanding our own financial problems, which are onerous and difficult, it is the desire of the government to assist you to the best of our ability, but we cannot in justice to the taxpayers of the dominion accept the statement of your requirements as outlined in Mr. Hart's letter of March 26 as representing a complete effort on your part to deal with your financial position.
We must, therefore, ask you to submit a revised program which will substantially reduce your contemplated deficit of $2,120,330.66 on ordinary account for the current year, which you anticipate notwithstanding your abandonment of sinking fund requirements which amounted to $2,421,620 last year.
As the preparation of this statement cannot be made until Mr. Hart returns to Victoria, and you appear to be in pressing need of immediate funds, we are prepared to advance such sums as may be necessary to meet your immediate and pressing requirements on the understanding that your revised program is to be submitted sometime within the next four or five weeks at the outside.
It would be desirable to ask you to submit a statement which would show something appoaching a balance on current account; however, realizing your difficulties and with the desire to be helpful, we will not go so far as to ask that this should be done, but we must expect the contemplated deficit to be reduced to something in the neighbourhood of $1,000,000 at the outside.
When we receive such a revised program, we will give it favourable consideration and you will be advised promptly as to whether we are prepared to make advances from time to time in conformity with your revised program up to the end of the current fiscal year.
Apart altogether from the justice of this request as affecting your province, may I point out that it has been our endeavour to deal with absolute fairness with the requests from each of the four western provinces and it would be most unfair if greater consideration should be shown to British Columbia than to any other province.
In all of these circumstances, I trust you will recognize the fairness of this proposal, and m accepting it recognize the fact that it is the best we can make.
I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that my object in referring to this communication is not to bring the problems of British Columbia before this house but to substantiate the statement I made that the Prime Minister and the government of Canada are requiring-and I think rightly so-from the government of British Columbia the right to review their accounts. We have guaranteed the borrowings of the Canadian Pacific Railway up to $60,000,000, and in the amendment which I am submitting to the house I say we have the right to that information from the Canadian Pacific Railway.

speechtext:
I am going to explain why, if hon. gentlemen will be patient. The motion deals exclusively with one subject, absolutely under the jurisdiction of this parliament, having regard to a railway undertaking owned and controlled by the government or the people of Canada. For the last three or four years it has been customary to introduce similar motions, dealing exclusively with the Canadian National Railways and its undertakings. The object of the amendment is to permit the house to go on with that inquiry into the affairs of the Canadian National Railways, but in addition it endeavours to bring in an entirely different enterprise that has nothing to do with the Canadian National Railways. I submit that if the motion is proper it is a substantive motion and should be brought before the house as such, with notice given in the ordinary way.
Therefore I would ask you, Mr. Speaker, to rule that the amendment is out of order at this time.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OP SELECT STANDING COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER ACCOUNTS AND ESTIMATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although this amendment undoubtedly refers to the committee the accounts of another institution I submit that this is quite in line with the work that has been carried on by that committee in the past, and which it is proposed shall be done by the committee this year. Last year the Prime Minister told us very distinctly that the Canadian National was not owned by the people of Canada but by the bondholders and that it was being carried forward for the sake of the bondholders. Yet we feel ourselves quite competent to conduct an investigation into the affairs of this company, nominally owned by the people of Canada but in reality owned by the bondholders.
I take it that the Canadian Pacific is in a very different position this year than has been the case in the past. Though it is a privately owned road it has come to this government to have its bonds guaranteed, with no opportunity for this house to examine the books of the company in order to ascertain whether or not that guarantee is needed ,or whether or not in the future a similar guarantee may be applied for. Surely parliament has the right to investigate anything of this nature; I think no one will deny that, and there could be no more appropriate committee than that which is investigating the affairs of the other corporation. I hope this amendment will not be ruled out of order on a mere technicality. It seems to me that it would be very far fetched to say we could not include a second railway in this motion.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS

speechtext:
The house resumed from Wednesday, May 2, consideration in committee of Bill No. 51, to improve the methods and practices of marketing of natural products in Canada and in export trade, and to make further provisions in connection therewith-Mr. Weir (Mel-fort)-Mr. Smith (Cumberland) in the chair.
On section 1-Short title.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose last, you will recall that I was discussing a monopoly of food products in Holland. Perhaps some explanation is necessary again as to why I went so far afield.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) brought down the budget the other day, and I thought he made a very creditable showing under the circumstances. You will recall, sir, that he spoke of the increase in commodity prices. It is unnecessary to repeat what he then said as to the increase that had taken place in the price of wheat, in the price of cattle and in the price of bacon hogs. He also gave us some very interesting statistics as to the increase of our export trade. If I remember correctly he said that we had had
Marketing Act

an average increase of around twenty per cent, and I felt that the minister was an apostle of cheer. Then the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture assured us that we ought to follow the world's trend. The Minister of Trade and Commerce assured us that we were in a new era, that all the world had commenced to regulate marketing by compulsory pools such as are contemplated by this bill. This morning I received, as did most hon. members, a monthly summary of the League of Nations, and on page 45 I find this question asked:
Whether there are any signs of recovery in world trade?
To this the answer is:
The total value of world trade has not diminished as much in 1933 as in previous years. Nevertheless it has continued to diminish by comparison with the corresponding figures of 1932, with the exception of a single month in which an improvement was shown in 1933 as compared with the previous year.
The other day the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) rapped me somewhat gently by stating that I had said that certain failures had occurred in connection with certain acts of a similar nature which had been passed in other countries. That was not my intention. I intended to give a general survey or summary of the legislation of this nature which had been passed throughout the world. The minister has better facilities than I to obtain this information. I advise the minister quite frankly to state now that the illustrations I gave were not always comparable to this legislation. I admit that very frankly. The minister knows just as I do that it is very difficult to distinguish among all these schemes. As he has very properly said, there are different conditions in the different countries. It is also necessary to distinguish among the crops of the various countries, whether they be deficiency or surplus crops. When the committee rose I was speaking of conditions in Holland and I should like to continue where I left off.
I was referring to the compulsory reduction in the hog population of that country. It will be recalled that the compulsory pool began with a population of 2,735,000; it was reduced to 2,000,000 and then finally to 1,800,000. Just how that was done furnishes an interesting side light on how these marketing bills work out. When a litter of pigs is born in Holland it is necessary for the farmer to buy a litter of tags. That was the best way discovered by the Dutch government of regulating production and conducting a hog marketing compulsory pool. The minister has stated that one of the objects of this bill

is the elimination of waste and the reduction of costs between production and consumption. These compulsory' pools bring about an increase in waste and cost. In order to administer the act in Holland it has been found necessary to have inspectors in every district, men who will keep in touch with production and prices. I regret to say that it is also' necessary to have an army of informers to report violations of the act.
The same condition applies to another pool in Holland known as the Dairy Crisis Central, which was established in June, 1932. I should like to have some information from the minister in connection with that pool. Its object was the usual one, that of raising prices to correspond with the cost of production. But what was the result? Naturally, the first result was an increase in prices and I assume the producers were very happy. But the next result was a decrease in the consumption of dairy products. The poor people had to live and probably without thinking they followed the law of necessity and turned to the consumption of other edible fats. What did the government do then? It taxed other edible fats. The government then insisted that milk fats should be mixed with oleomargarine. They had to provide for the consumption of milk. Thus it goes from one step to another. I should like the minister to tell me if I am right. I observe from the press, I think the London Economist, that they have recently passed a law prohibiting people from growing fruits and vegetables in their own gardens. From one step to another in order to make a monopoly successful.
I should like to draw the attention of the minister to conditions in Roumania. An agricultural marketing act was passed in 1931 which gave a syndicate control over the whole grain marketing system. Those who are interested in this bill might obtain some very significant information from what happened in that country. That act was abolished within a month because a new government came into office. The new government decided upon an entirely different system but it was still a marketing monopoly. They made provision for a national agricultural trading company, a union of cereal exporters, a millers' central office and a millers' syndicate. The provisions worked out in the usual way. A tax was placed on bread but the bakers felt that they could not absorb that tax. The mayors of the municipalities, rather than have the people starve, passed laws that the price of bread should not be increased. There was then a strike of the bakers and the government finally was forced

Marketing Act
to have the military bake-shops take over the making of bread. There were abuses by the producers who were to secure these export benefits. Rye was mixed with wheat and other abuses occurred. The government finally ran out of money and the monopoly was abolished on April 22, 1932.
The minister could secure some very valuable information from Italy. That country has gone in for producers monopolies. I do not intend to run over the whole list but I would point out to the minister the difficulties which have arisen in connection with the rice monopoly. In that case there were the usual results, increased prices at first, then decreased consumption and finally the necessity of decreasing the acreage. The Italian government is faced with the problem of how to bring about that reduction, whether it shall be a flat reduction in acreage or the putting of the least fertile lands out of commission and preventing the least competent farmers from growing rice. That is a very live issue in Italy to-day. The same conditions exist in Spain. In November, 1927, the government formed a syndicate or cooperative group of producers of rice. That group had very much the same powers contemplated by this bill. At first the legislation applied only to the growers of rice within certain provinces. In
1929	it was found necessary to make it compulsory on all rice growers and on March 6,
1930	it was abolished. The minister will remember that I am simply trying to cover a vast territory as quickly as possible and therefore I can give very little detail. I would have him bear in mind the position of Switzerland. There was a wheat marketing monopoly in Switzerland, beginning in 1915- a long while ago, practically at the outset of the war. It ran along until 1929. There were objections from both producers and consumers alike. Now, the Minister of Justice knows that Switzerland is a very democratic country, in some respects the most democratic in the world. They had a system of referendum and they took one as to whether their marketing monopoly should continue or not, and on March 3, 1929 the people of Switzerland voted upon the subject and decided upon the repeal of that marketing monopoly.
Let me now take the minister to Hungary, where there is a cooperative society called the Futura. It is supposed to deal with all agricultural products, and it dealt particularly with wheat. It has had a chequered career, and, so far as I know, it is still in existence; but the last word that I can find of it is that the money collected for the purpose of being
given to the producers had to be used to buy food for people who were starving.
It seems a long way from the wheat fields of the Saskatchewan to the cotton fields of the Nile, but in both places there are people who seem to think that there is magic. The Egyptians are noted for their magic. They tried to repeal the law of supply and demand some time ago-in 1921-because they believed it was a shibboleth. What happened? They began to sustain the cotton market, buying cotton, and the price went down and down so that in 1931 the condition became so bad that the international federation of cotton spinners and manufacturers went to the government. I should like to have the evidence of what took place at that interview. Presumably the buyers of cotton said, "The price is going down because of the supplies you are holding over the market; you have a market monopoly." But whatever took place, in 1931 the Egyptian government gave up the idea of destroying supply and demand by legislative magic and announced that it was out of the market. It had had enough of marketing legislation. There is still a problem, because in May, 1932, the government held 387,000 bales of cotton and was afraid to sell it.
In Jugoslavia there was partial control of wheat and rye from May, 1930, but that was not satisfactory. In June, 1931, provision was made for a monopoly. In March, 1932, after only a few months' experience, the idea of monopoly control was abandoned.
I wonder whether it is necessary to go on. In Uruguay they had marketing monopoly legislation, and that
Marketing Act

in that it promotes organized buying on a similar scale or what is equally effective in the buyers' interest, taking their supplies from spot stocks weekly, semi-weekly or even daily, and at the prevailing market price at the time, or if a low price opportunity offers, rapidly picking up a huge block of butter and subsequently remaining out of the buying market for a period. The price may rise temporarily as a result of purchases of this kind, but the inactivity of some of the big buyers over a period of a few weeks invariably results in a downward swing of prices.
Could anything be plainer? We have to look ahead. I know the minister has investigated this matter, but it seems to me he ought to have his investigations printed for us so that we might follow his arguments. With the information I have at present I must say the thing is incomprehensible.
While I have Mr. Stevens' publication before me I want to refer to another matter. We are rather well thought of in Great Britain because we have not had these marketing monopolies. I am going to prove that statement from Mr. Stevens' publication. The same writer, Mr. Wilson, in the same article but speaking of cheese, has this to say:
The freedom of trading that has obtained in connection with Canadian products, in contrast to that which has developed with most of the other exporting countries, is a factor that is appreciated in the United Kingdom, and assists very materially in maintaining and developing goodwill.
I mentioned that subject when I spoke on the principle of the bill, and I think it was the hon. member for Dauphin who said he could not follow me. I am sorry, because I like the hon. member for Dauphin and I would like to follow him in that matter, but surely both of us can follow the report of our own commissioner, who is a trained man on the ground and who reports on these matters, and when we follow him we ought to follow his advice.
Now I want to return to Mr. Amery and his publication, and this is something that has a wider bearing. He comes now to discuss the principles of socialism; the report says:
During the lifetime of the socialist government there was considerable discussion of bulk purchase by import boards. Though there was at no time any very clear definition of the manner in which the policy would be carried out. obviously it visualies that the whole supplies of certain commodities would be purchased either by a department of state or by some statutory corporation created for the purpose.

Marketing Act

I presume the same argument that follows applies to selling as well as to buying. The report continues:
We see obvious objections to bulk purchase by the state or by some statutory body created for the purpose by the state. Under such a system every purchase might raise a diplomatic issue and, accordingly, give rise to controversy with foreign and even with empire governments. The subsequent distribution of the commodities bought in bulk might easily lead to serious internal political difficulties and there might be grave financial risks to the state arising out of the popular pressure for goods to be sold at a rate below the proper economic price.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I am going to stop to remind the committee that this report is published by the Empire Economic Union; it is not a statement by the hon. member for Weyburn or by myself. The report continues:
In addition bulk purchase might have a serious effect on world prices.
Now see the implication, as far as it affects this bill. The report goes on:
The establishment of the federal farm board in the United States of America and the existence of the wheat pool in Canada both appear to have had this effect. The knowledge that these two bodies were holding great quantities of wheat made all dealers in wheat nervous, as they could never be certain when heavy unloading would take place. The view is widely held that when large stocks in the hands of a few are hanging over the market, there must inevitably be a depressing effect on prices.
I know these matters are controversial, but after all this should not be a time for speculation; we ought to know. We ought to have the evidence, and we should not go on until we do know. There is another feature with which the report of the union deals, and I am glad it does so. It has to do with a matter to which I have given very serious study, and that is what happens when a mistake is made in big business, when one man, be he the head of a marketing board or the head of a great industrial concern, makes a mistake. That is what you will have to consider when you have centralized marketing. The report goes on to deal with that very question:
There is a general objection to unified purchase of any commodity by the government or any publicly controlled body.
Again I repeat that the argument applies to sale as well as to purchase.
It demonstrated itself very clearly during the war, when this method was employed for wheat, sugar and many other commodities. The objection arises through the fallibility of human judgment. Members of purchasing boards have to make up their minds from time to time as to the market position of any commodity, and have to come to their conclusions; however ably

they may be composed, their number is obviously limited, and their judgment, however intelligently informed, may be mistaken. For instance, if a board makes up its mind that wheat is going to rise in price and purchases the entire requirements of a country on this basis while events prove that world markets instead of rising, fall, the error of judgment is transferred on a huge scale and involves enormous sums. With the present practice, there are many individual buyers-
Or sellers, I may add.
-some will take one view and some the opposite, and which ever is right or wrong some kind of average result which is not so far from the actual truth will be arrived at, and therefore the amount of error in either direction will never become of an extravagant nature.
Had I time I think I could show that this is one of the reasons why we have the depth of our agricultural depression to-day. We have had these monopoly boards, these producers' boards, with compulsory cooperation in marketing, so generally throughout the world that the world now lags behind us in recovery, because we better preserved our competitive spirit.
There is another fallacy to which I should like to refer. I have heard it said that now the producers are to have control of their own produce. Well, could there be any greater fallacy than that? The dominion marketing board will not produce; it is the farmer who produces, and he is to lose control and to be deprived of the right to exercise his business judgment. I am not saying this measure deprives him; as I am aware, this is an enabling measure, but it will enable some producers-the majority if you like-to deprive him of the exercise of his business judgment. He is to become the ward of the state. What is left to him? If he cannot sell the product of his toil? What has he left? Of course he may have his land and his debts, but he has lost his credit. By this measure you are taking his credit from him. That has followed legislation of this kind which has been enacted in Europe.
I see some hon. gentlemen-and I believe they are all sitting opposite-who I fancy have money to loan. Oh, I see one on this side, too. Would any one of you loan money to a man who could not dispose of his product? I have no desire to enter into a credit controversy. We have had several of them lately. But I must ask: Who would lend money over a period of time to a man who, you knew, might not be able to dispose of his product? He could not borrow on his business judgment, because that is taken out of his hands. He has his land, and he works.

Marketing Act
The other day one of my friends to my left said that the wheat farmers in the west were becoming peasants. Well, I do not wish to exaggerate, but I must say that in this legislation I can see nothing but serfdom. We had it years ago, and we are going back not to the nineteenth century but back to the days of monopolies, to the days which men rightly or wrongly called the Dark Ages. This bill is not without support from the big interests. They have their monopolies, and we have on our statute books legislation against monopolies. I should like to ask the minister if he will keep that legislation on the statute books once we pass this bill. Can you put one set of men in prison because they are operating a monopoly and another set in prison because of competition? Surely we should do more than simply discuss the details of this bill clause by clause. We should consider all its implications. I can think of the support which this bill will receive from some of my friends who are engaged in monopolies, and I am reminded of the invitation the spider gave to the fly, particularly when in the bill we have a provision in regard to shutting out competition from foreign lands.
I have gone on longer than I had intended, but I wish to say simply this, that although I should have liked to help in framing this bill, I have no heart for the job. I am opposed to the principle. I have an idea that the bill cannot be properly framed either by Conservatives or by Liberals. It is a socialist bill, and I would turn it over to the socialists. I have no heart for lighting a crucible, moulding men, and destroying individuality. I have no heart for that sort of thing in an economic way any more than in a national way. I plead with the government to hesitate, to consider and to ask themselves in view of the fact that we are pulling out of the depression if it is necessary to sacrifice the economic and social life of this country.

Well, it is one of the leading commercial bodies in Canada. It represents large interests, and points out that there are two principles in this bill which should be carefully considered. The first is coercion and the second compulsion. I quote from a communication which has been received by hon. members:
It seems to the council that there are two main principles applied in Bill No. 51. First, the granting to a "reasonable number" of those interested in a particular commodity in a special district, the right to coerce the remainder of those so interested. The rights of individuals to control and dispose of their own property and the rights of minorities, have always been jealously guarded under our political and legal systems. The Agricultural Marketing Act of Great Britain, which is said to have served as a model for Bill No. 51, recognizes and respects these two classes of rights. The British act requires not only that the minister of the department satisfy himself as to the reasonableness of any "development" scheme put forward by an interested group, but the whole scheme, together with the evidence upon which the minister has based his judgment, must be laid before both houses of parliament. The most complete publicity is also provided for with regard to these schemes, and in certain cases a system of arbitration is provided for those aggrieved by the acts of the development boards. It is respectfully urged by the council of the board of trade that the rights of minorities and of individuals be accorded the same protection under Bill No. 51 as they receive in the British Agricultural Marketing Act.
The second principle underlying Bill No. 51 is the securing of compensation to those who suffer loss by any action of the proposed marketing boards. This compensation, in the
opinion of the council, should be a charge upon all those engaged in the particular trade in which the compensation is awarded. Under no circumstances should the funds of the dominion be used to provide compensation to special interests, or to meet the expenses involved in the operation of the act other than those of administration and the necessary expenses of the dominion marketing board. Each trade, this council believes, should stand on its own feet in the matter of costs involved and in the assistance extended to it.
I will not read much more from this memorandum, addressed to the Prime Minister and to members of both houses, but there is another paragraph which I think is well worth noting:
The council of the board of trade recognizes that the methods of grading and packing of natural products both for home and overseas and foreign markets, are legitimate subjects for legislation, but at the same time, the council wishes to point out that this field of legislative activity is already adequately covered in so far as many products are concerned, and the gaps could be filled in easily by supplementary legislation.

When I draw my indemnity I have to take oath as to how many days I have been away from the house. I do not think any member should have to take an oath on a matter of that kind. Such a thing is not asked by any large corporation in this country, and I cannot see why it should be asked of a member of parliament. I have heard judges' deploring that the oath is used so extensively in this country as to become almost farcical, that people hardly take it seriously. When I was elected I pointed out to my constituents that I would have to answer to them, not to the accountant's office of the House of Commons. I think this provision should be removed from our statutes if it is a statutory provision. I sincerely believe that it is not fair to members of parliament and to parliament as a whole that a member when he gets his indemnity cheque should have to take an oath. When I was elected I was receiving an indemnity of 84,000; it is $3,600 now. I seldom miss any sittings of the house, and yet I am sincere in my protest. I do not think that the full oath should be taken when members draw their indemnities to which they are absolutely entitled. No financial institution of any kind insists upon it, and if there is one office that should accept the word of members of the house it is the accountant's office of the House of Commons.

Towards the close of last session the matter was referred to some of the officials of the pension commission and I was asked, on the eve of my departure for my own section of the country, whether I could take it up with them. Unfortunately I had to leave in rather a hurry for Cochrane but I received a letter to the effect that the case would not be reopened. Two years ago I quoted from some fairly strong editorials appearing in the newspapers, some of them of Conservative and independent tendencies, and I called attention particularly to an editorial in the Porcupine Advance, which had been fighting for this man for several years. In my riding there is a large body of returned soldiers and only three or four at most have failed to receive the attention they deserve.
The minister is always willing to listen to the returned man's plea, and I am sure that if he knew all the facts he would grant this man a new hearing immediately. Not only the House of Commons but the whole country welcomed the statement made by the Prime Minister almost at the beginning of the session with reference to certain cases brought to the attention of the house by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth and the hon. member for Vancouver Centre. Those cases I believe were dealt with immediately. I wish that I could present Mr. Hussin's case as forcefully as the hon. members I refer to presented the cases in which they were interested, because I believe that the matter would have received attention at once from the minister and the department.
If I understand the act rightly it gives sufficient leeway to allow this case to be reopened. It is my duty now, unless I get a promise from the minister that it will be reopened, to put once more on the record of parliament exactly what has taken place with regard to this man. speakeroldname: Hon. MURRAY MacLAREN (Minister of Pensions and National Health):
speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Extended reference to this case was made by the hon. gentleman last year and I then said that I would see that it was again thoroughly investigated. The man was brought from his home in the northern section of Ontario to Christie street hospital in Toronto and special arrangements were made so that his case should be fully looked into. He was examined by two nerve specialists, one belonging to the department and the other a specialist in nervous disorders who had no relation with the department. The case was completely reviewed and the man thoroughly examined, and the report of the two specialists was that it was a case of malingery. I can understand my hon. friend holding the view that the case has not been fairly dealt with. That frequently occurs in cases such as hysteria and malingery; there is always a doubt, especially on the part of those connected or associated with the man. As I say, the report of those two specialists was that it was a case of malingery. It is also stated that there was repeated evidence that he worked as a labourer between the years 1919 and 1931. The result was that it was not considered a genuine case and he was not awarded a pension. I made every effort to have this man examined in an impartial way and by men specially trained and qualified in diseases of the kind, and that was the result. I had hopes that my friend who has now again brought this case forward might feel that the examination was a fair one, and that the result was arrived at by men well qualified to reach a right conclusion.
There is no limit to reexaminations, even if it seems not very necessary,-because this man has been examined again and again. My friend asks whether I will arrange for a further examination. I say that notwithstanding all

I have some interesting facts, Mr. Chairman, with regard to the payment of pensions which I think I should make known, as the information is rather important. I wish to place it on Hansard so that hon. gentlemen may have an opportunity of studying the figures with greater ease. The reason I do so is that frequently the criticism is heard that pensions are being reduced. I am not surprised that this view is held by many, and there may be a certain diminution in the amount of pension paid, but that diminution is not large. There are two principal reasons for this misapprehension, but before I make my statement I should like to describe how the representative of the treasury board keeps his record of pension payments, so that hon. gentlemen will be a little better able to follow the short explanation I have to make.
The representative of the treasury board, who is the bookkeeper and paymaster, as it were, has three columns in his records with regard to the payment of pensions. There are three classifications under which pensions are placed, and the three added together show the total payments. First is the column showing the regular monthly payments; this is an amount that is more or less the same subject to minor changes. As I say, this figure is fairly constant, though not necessarily so because pensions are subject to change. Many people say, "My pension was so much a year ago and now it is so much less." Pensions are subject to change in accordance with the amount of disability. Naturally if a man has lost an eye or both eyes that is a permanent disability and his pension does not change. If a man has an amputation that is a permanent disability and there is no change
in his pension. There are innumerable other conditions, however, such as bronchitis, rheumatism, myalgia and all that sort of thing, which vary from time to time, and the pen-: sion varies with the amount of disability.
The second column refers to retroactive adjustments, which I mentioned to my hon. friend from Prince. This amount varies also. Before taking my seat I should like to indicate one other point, namely that the average amount of pensions paid is considerably lower. The explanation is one which should be known to all hon. members. As I pointed out when speaking about the restoration of pensions, under the amendment to the act made in 1930 the small pensioners were restored-and by that I mean the pensioners between five per cent and fourteen per cent. As a result hundreds and hundreds have been restored, thereby increasing very substantially the total number of pensioners. But the increase in the number of pensioners is largely caused by the number who are drawing small pensions between five per cent and fourteen per cent, and for that reason-I give this information for what it is worth-the average amount of pension paid to-day is less than it was.

I understand that a quorum of the pension commission travels around the country and holds hearings at certain points. My difficulty is that it is very
[Mr. MacLaren.l

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: As a matter of fact the information can be obtained with great ease. A schedule is drawn up several weeks ahead and can always be obtained. If any hon. member of the committee wishes such information I shall see that he receives it at once. The regular procedure is to write the pension commission and inquire when they will sit at a certain place. The chief pensions adviser always has that information. There is a schedule somewhat like a time table, but perhaps a little more variable, which is always ready for weeks ahead. If the hon. member would write the pension commission he would get the information.

I have not been able to get it by writing. The soldiers' adviser will

say that there may be a session at such and such a place next spring, but he does not know. I had real difficulty in finding out when they would reach a certain point.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I think the hon. member will find that that information is known several weeks ahead.

I understood the minister to say that the pensions were progressively becoming smaller. I would ask if it is the policy of the department progressively to diminish pensions, and if so, upon what authority they are making this change. I have in mind several types of cases that certainly occur from time to time, and just how it is possible for the department progressively to reduce pensions consistently with the act I do not understand.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
So far as I am aware
there is no policy of reducing pensions, and further the department could not properly have any such policy because the amount of pension granted is according to the degree of disability. The disability is assessed, not by the department, but by the pension commission, which is practically an independent body. The department has nothing whatever to do with any reduction of pension, and so far as I am aware there has been no move in that direction.

What about the reduction
in the pensions of dependents, which are not awarded according to the degree of disability? I know cases where dependents have had their pensions reduced, and I am not referring to cases, for instance, where there is a reduction because of a child coming of age. I have in mind a dependent's pension to a widow, and that pension was certainly reduced. How does that operate?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: If my hon. friend from Gloucester would give me specific cases I should be pleased to have them looked into and give him a proper answer. So far as I am aware these cases do not arise. Of course, there may be a case like this, where a widow who has been receiving a pension for some years remarries.

It is not that kind of a
case at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Outside of that the
pensions that are awarded to dependent fathers and mothers depend upon their financial position, and if a dependent father or mother gets into better circumstances I can understand the pension being reduced. But I shall be glad to look into any case of which my hon. friend from Gloucester will give me the particulars.

Here is a case in point. A widowed mother was receiving a pension on account of her son who was killed at the front. After enjoying that pension for several years she was suddenly notified that the pension was being reduced from forty to twenty dollars a month, and her condition at the time she received that notice was just as bad as it was when she was receiving a pension of forty dollars a month. The pension board or the department must have some way of looking into the matter and making a report on such cases. I do not know who reported on this case, but whoever did make the report made a false report because I am personally acquainted with these people; I know their conditions and everything connected with them. I took the matter up and reported the case as T knew it, and as the clergyman of the district knew it, and as a result the pension board added to the reduced pension something like ten dollars. Now, I do not want any pension board to add to a reduced pension on my recommendation. I do not make recommendations. I want every case treated on its merits, and the reason I am bringing this question up to-night is for the guidance of the pension board in the future. In all cases the pension board should see that a proper investigation is held; they should not depend on their agents getting reports from Tom, Dick and Harry, without going to the spot and seeing the actual conditions for themselves.
To prove my contention I would remind the minister that some seven or eight years ago it was the practice to send lady inspectors around to see the condition of the pensioners and see if the pensions, especially of dependents, should be continued on the scale first granted. One of these lady inspectors called at my home on a Sunday afternoon, showed me a list of names of people she was to visit in my county, and asked me where they were located. I gave her all the addresses and told her how to reach these places. One of the cases was about a mile and a quarter from my home, and she asked' me if I would give her the particulars in connection with that dependent family because she wanted to make her report and send it out the next day. She did not visit that family and make her own report. She made a report on the word of Tom, Dick and Harry, and that widowed pensioner had her pension reduced after losing a son in the flying corps at the front. That was the practice some years ago. Lately I have not heard much about it except in the one case I now mention.

The other day I received a letter from a pensioner in my county, sending me a notice that his pension had been cut from twenty-five dollars to ten dollars. He is a returned soldier trying to make a living on the farm. On whose report was his pension cut? I have made inquiries and I tried to find out as much as possible when I returned home at Easter. It was reported in the neighborhood that this man's pension had been reduced because it was found that he had a couple of horses and a cow. What right have they to reduce his pension as a returned soldier because he happens to have a couple of horses and a cow? If he was entitled to a pension of twenty-five dollars a month they had no right to cut it down because he was trying to make a living on his little farm where he has been able to raise two horses and a cow; but the pension was cut down from twenty-five to ten dollars a month, and he had to go on the relief list and get relief for himself and his cattle to keep them from starving. It was robbing Peter to pay Paul.
These are two cases. I do not wish to give the names before this committee, but I shall be glad to give them to the minister any time he wants them.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: If the hon. member for Gloucester will be good enough to give me the names in confidence I shall have the cases looked into.
I will do that.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: There is a little more to say about it. It is suggested that the man had his pension reduced because he had two horses and a cow. I know nothing about the case; I do not remember having heard of it, but I cannot believe that the pension was reduced for that reason. If he had a hundred cows and fifty horses his pension would be just the same. There must be some other reason, and I hope the hon. member for Gloucester will give me a chance to look into the matter. These cases are investigated, but it might be exacting a higher standard than is found in other positions in life to expect that those investigating always do their duty. I should like to be satisfied as to whether the case the hon. member mentioned has been actually investigated; the records will show. Both cases will be thoroughly looked into.

With all due deference to the minister I question whether his explanation as to the reduction in pensions gives us a true picture. Every hon. member knows from the correspondence he has received, as does everyone who is interested in returned

soldier matters that outside of the reinstatement of pensions which had been settled by a final payment there has been quite a substantial cut in pensions. I am not saying that in some cases that cut has not been justified, but I do say that the minister is not correct when he says that the reason the average is reduced is the fact that some small pensioners who had received final payments have now been restored to monthly pensions. Letter after letter is received by hon. members of this house, by the legion and by others interested in ex-service men's problems, to the effect that pensions have been reduced. As I say, some reductions may be justified, but do not let us fool ourselves about it. I understand that for some reason the auditor general has gone down to the pension commissioners or to the minister's department and started an investigation as to the legality of the amounts awarded for pensions.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: With the pension commission.
Does the minister say that the auditor general did not institute an investigation?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: It is the routine examination he makes in all departments. He does not come into the department to investigate as to the propriety of awarding pensions.
He does not?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: So far as I know it is limited to the pension commission.

I think the minister and I understand each other perfectly well; the department does not award pensions, it is the board of pension commissioners. The minister can correct me if I am wrong, but I understand that the auditor general or his representative has gone over the files to find out whether or not he considers a pensioner entitled to a pension. Will the minister tell me whether that is right?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I think that is correct.

I submit-I am speaking in the presence of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie)-that that is an absolutely incorrect function of the auditor general. I submit that he has no more right to overrule a decision of the board of pension commissioners than he has to overrule the exchequer court if it decides that the crown is liable for the payment of a certain sum of money. The commission has the statutory authority, and it seems to me the auditor general has no jurisdiction whatever. This is one case

Supply-Pensions-European War
of reduction of pensions which has been referred to. I understand that the auditor general has gone over the files and stated that such and such a man received his disability before service, and suggesting that his disability was only an aggravation of a prewar disability and that, therefore, he was not entitled to the full amount, notwithstanding the fact that the statute awards such a man the full amount if he served overseas in a theatre of war. I submit that is one of the reasons why pensions have been cut.
I understand that some 70,000 files have been reviewed by the board of pension commissioners. The other night we had a statement to the effect that the records show that reductions had occurred in something like two or three thousand cases. In the face of that I do not see how the minister can say that pensions have not been reduced, even in view of the fact that there are more pensioners now through the restoration of a number of small pensioners.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I did not say that.

That is the impression
that was left on my mind. I am glad I spoke and have had that impression removed. There is no doubt that pensions have been reduced considerably in a great number of cases. I have had experiences similar to those of the hon. member for Gloucester. Just to-night I received a letter indicating that a parents' pension of two old people in my constituency had been reduced from $30 to $10. In another case two old people, not in my constituency, were receiving the munificent sum of $10 a month. The two boys of this father and mother are dead in France, so there is no question as to the connection between service and disability. They are now sleeping in Flanders fields, and these two old people are receiving $10 a month. I saw the file in this case. Someone had suggested that the award be $20 a month in respect of the death of the two sons, both of whom had assigned pay, but someone else had put a red ink line through the "twenty" and put down "ten." The case was finally re-examined the other day and they are now receiving $20. That is the kind of case the hon. member for Gloucester is complaining about, the case in regard to which it takes months to get recognition by the investigators. Many of these people are probably in a worse position and deserve more from the country than some men who are partially disabled. These particular two old people have lost their two sons and it seems to me that the country ought not to be ungrateful and should see that they and others similarly situated should 74726-1795
be provided with sufficient for their maintenance. I think the minister should look into the administration of dependents' pensions. As I understand it there is no appeal in the case of a dependent's pension unless it is on the question as to whether or not death was due to service. The question of the financial position of the applicant cannot be considered by the court of appeal; the question whether or not the son or sons would have supported the parents had they lived cannot be referred to the court of appeal; the question whether these parents have sufficient income to provide the necessaries of life cannot be referred to the court. I submit that these cases should be within the jurisdiction of the court of appeal because many of them constitute the most distressing cases with which we have to deal.
There is another matter which the minister and I have discussed before, the matter of the married cases. He will remember the other night when we were discussing this matter I intimated along with other members that I thought many of these cases could not be dealt with simply by reference to the Department of Justice. I intimated that there are cases in connection with which legislation would have to be passed, and I should like to know the position of the minister in connection with this matter. I understand that generally one does not forecast legislation, but it seems to me that the committee is entitled to know what the minister has in mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I should like to make a
statement with reference to the cases referred to by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yar-mouth (Mr. Ralston). Up to April 28 there had been submitted to the Department of Justice, 163 married cases. My understanding is that there are some 570 in all to be submitted. Yesterday my deputy minister received a letter from the chairman of the pension commission stating:
The commission have forwarded to you quite a number of files with regard to the material status of pensioners. I am writing accordingly to let you know that the review of these cases will not be completed even by the end of the year. You may expect to receive each week about the same number you have been receiving in the past. It is quite probable that with regard to the out of Canada pensioners the review will not be completed until another year.
We have made a pretty careful review of the cases we have already received and they seem to resolve themselves into about four different categories, or perhaps five. After having examined them with some care, the question is, what are we going to do about

them? Out of the 163 cases there are about thirty-three in which the parties have not shown good faith with respect to alleged marriages; that is the opinion of the law officers of the department. There are about sixteen that could be remedied for the future by the pensioner and his alleged wife going through a form of marriage, provided the Pension Act were amended to permit such marriage. I added together the numbers the minister gave, and I took the report to include 117 cases out of 163.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not desire to go into the various groups because we may have to change the wording somewhat. In group 1 there are twenty-five definite cases.
Is the minister reversing the order? Twenty-five happened to be the last figure he mentioned a moment ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In subclause 1 of group 1 there are twenty-five; in subclause 2 there are nineteen; in subclause 3 there are three. There is some distinction between them all. In group 2 they have placed definitely sixty-three; in group 3, eighteen; and in group 3 (a) there are nine cases. In group 4 there are nine cases which may be increased to thirty-two in all. I think they have dealt now with the whole 163 and divided them into four groups, some of which have had to be subdivided owing to particular circumstances that have arisen.

Accepting the minister's
reservation, that the wording may be changed, it appears that there are sixteen out of 163 in which a new form of marriage, provided the statute were amended, would meet the situation. In forty-three the onus is on the commission, from which I take it at this stage that the marriages are presumed to be valid. There are twenty-five more that might
[Mr. Guthrie.l
be in that class. That makes, out of 163, eighty-four altogether in which it would appear that the parties have merits. I understood the minister to say that in thirty-three cases a want of good faith was shown.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There are thirty-one in which the parties have not shown good faith with respect to the alleged marriages, in the opinion of the officers who examined the files.

I have taken the position, to which I adhere, that the cases I am particularly interested in, whether I know the persons or not, are cases in which the parties have lived together believing they were man and wife, and where the community recognized them as such; they have discharged the duties and responsibilities of married life, taking care of the children and the man supporting the woman; and the money which the country has paid has been devoted to the purpose for which it was intended. If there are cases in which good faith does not appear then I should say that at any rate they are the last cases to be looked after. I hope however that the Minister of Justice can go further-I quite understand the work involved -and give us some idea as to what might be proposed. I realize that he went some distance the other night in intimating his opinion, which he was careful to say was not the opinion of the government, that legislation would have to be provided and that these cases of good faith ought to be looked after. I want to urge not only upon the Minister of Justice but upon the Minister of Pensions and the government as well the opinion that it is absolutely necessary, in decency and propriety, for this country to look after these cases. I do not believe we can afford to have the board of pension commissioners bastardize children or call people adulterers who have lived together in circumstances in which the community is recognizing them as man and wife. It is an unfortunate situation that has arisen, and we in this house should do all we can to correct it as soon as possible. That is all I say at the moment.
There is something else however which I want to say to the Minister of Pensions with regard to the way in which the undertaking given by the Prime Minister has been carried out, at least in some instances. I brought this to the minister's attention and I do not think he will want me to put it on record. The Prime Minister made a statement in this house, and I have every reason to accept his words absolutely at their face value because I believe he meant them. He said that those

Supply-Pensions-European War
pensions would be restored where they had been taken away without notice-in all cases. That will be found at page 538.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Did he say in all cases?
Yes, he made no exceptions.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understood that an arbitrary date was fixed-all cases arising since the 1st of February, 1933.

I think the Minister of Justice is quite right in saying that there was such an understanding. I do not think it is mentioned in the Prime Minister's statement, but everyone understood that that was what he was referring to. I have therefore no objection to that reservation being made. But we were dealing particularly with marriage cases in which there was alleged invalidity of marriage, and other cases were included in which the pension had been reduced in cases where there should have been a hearing.
I asked him if those were included and I understood they were.

I believe the ex-Postmaster General asked the Prime Minister that and he received that answer. The other day I came across a case which made the hair stand up on the back of my neck a little. I found the board of pension commissioners writing back to a man who had had his pension cut off in order to repay alleged overpayments, and what they wrote him was that the Prime Minister's statement referred only to cases where there had been a marriage, "and in your case," they said, "there was not a marriage." I understood the Prime Minister's statement to refer to any case in which the cancellation or withholding of the pension was 'due to the question having been raised as to the validity of the marriage or as to the legality of the state in which husband and wife were living. Yet this officer of the board of pension commissioners writes back to say, "Well, the Prime Minister's statement referred only to marriages and did not have reference to your case, because there was no marriage." The point about the board of pension commissioners' objection to paying the pension was that the marriage was not valid; in other words, that there was no marriage. And they were saying, "In your case there was no ceremony and therefore the Prime Minister's statement does not apply." I brought the matter to the attention of the minister. I shall not give the name, but the minister has it. We found that he, an old man
living in Toronto, had sent in to the board of pension commissioners in 1917 a form setting forth the name and date of birth of the child, and1 that that had been acknowledged under date of October 18, 1917, by the board. On June 27, 1918, the board sent him this letter:
I have the honour, by direction, to return herewith your certificate of marriage, the same having been perused is no longer required by this commission.
They continued to pay him pension until 1932 or 1933, when they discovered that his wife had been married before. They asked for a statement as to the death of the previous husband, and, being unable to get it, cut off his pension and charged him with a lot of back pension. A reference to the file will show that what the man did was to send to them, in good faith and aboveboard, as he says, a statement of the facts: he told them he had not gone through a church marriage, but he had cuttings from a newspaper, "Answers to Correspondents" saying that under certain circumstances where parties constantly live together as husband and wife-called marriages of habit and repute-that is a good marriage. He had that from a newspaper, I think the Glasgow Herald. He also had a statement from the newspaper that promise of marriage followed by consummation on the faith of the promise was sufficient. He said that under these circumstances they considered themselves married. They had sent to Glasgow the report of the birth of their daughter in 1917, and enclosed a clipping showing the birth. He sent in the certificate he had previously forwarded to the board, which turned out to be the certificate which they had acknowledged in the letter I have just read and which apparently had been signed by the two of them, believing that that was sufficient to constitute a marriage. This was the paper acknowledged by the board as a certificate of marriage in 1918. They had accepted it; and if the Minister of National Defence were in his place I think he would appreciate this, because he brought up a case the other night of the board of pension commissioners having accepted proof of marriage for years and years and then repudiating it. They had accepted this, had gone on paying him, and then suddenly stopped his pension and claimed over payments. He wrote me a letter in which he said:
You will note wTe were married by consent and licence only.
And he said that they had been entirely aboveboard in connection with the whole
2832	COMMONS
Supply-Pensions-European War
matter, and had advised the board of pension commissioners that they did not go through a clerical ceremony. The board of pension commissioners, notwithstanding the undertaking of the Prime Minister, deliberately wrote to that man and told him in effect that the Prime Minister's undertaking did not apply to him. This is the letter, dated April 10, 1934:
Reference is made to your communication of April 2, referring to a statement made by the hon. the Prime Minister to the effect that all additional pension should be restored in cases where the validity of a marriage is in question. This refers only to persons who have actually contracted marriage.
According to the records of this commission you have at no time contracted marriage with the person with whom you are now residing and under such circumstances the commissioners have no authority under the act to award additional pension.
And this notwithstanding the fact that the board in 1918 had seen and acknowledged the certificate of marriage that he sent in at that time, and had been paying him ever since. My information from those who know this man in Toronto is that the community regard these people as man and wife; there has never been a breath of suspicion as to that, yet the board of pension commissioners not only refuse to recognize the marriage but even refuse to recognize the undertaking of the Prime Minister. It is annoying and irritating, when the Prime Minister has attempted to give this country and the ex-service men the assurance which he was honestly giving and which I know he fully intends to carry out, to have the board of pension commissioners writing chiseling letters of that kind to detract from the undertaking.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
While one cannot say
definitely what was in the mind of the Prime Minister, from the language I heard him use my own judgment is that the case my hon. friend refers to is one of those which he intended should be included in the statement he made. But whether in his mind he would exclude a case of that kind I cannot say.

The Prime Minister said on page 538 of Hansard:
Might I say to the hon. gentleman that the government has already determined, as I indicated in part this afternoon, that in all those cases where men's pensions were taken from them without notice, they should be restored. That has been decided. The method by which it is to be done, whether by legislation or otherwise, is a matter on which I ventured to ask the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) about to-day. I believe under the provisions of the Relief Act we may be able to accomplish it. It is proposed to be done if it can.

In most of the cases I know about, except these few, that has been done; the Prime Minister has found a way to do it. I need hardly say it is not the Prime Minister I am blaming. What I do complain of is this disposition to irritate people and be as niggardly as possible in connection with a matter as to which I think we should be fairly generous.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
May I clear up a few
of these points? First there is a difference of opinion about the date, February 1, 1933.
Back to what date does the minister say the Prime Minister's undertaking applies?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I am not submitting my view. I have said that these matters were referred to the Department of Justice.. I have drawn attention to the statements made by the Prime Minister in the house, and the Minister of Justice, so that an interpretation and decision may be given on that point. I have views about it, but I am not making the decision.
As to what is to be done, I believe that these marriage cases will finally-it is evidently going to take some time-be disposed of in a fairly satisfactory way. I have not said by legislation or by what means, but my present view is that this matter will be satisfactorily dealt with.
Meanwhile it seems to me that we are overlooking the condition at the present time. With only one or two exceptions that I know of, these cases are now receiving their pay and allowances. board of pension commissioners were far from complimentary. They said that these were cases which should never have been allowed to drag so long. The Skitch case began in 1923, and from that time dragged on through the courts. It ran between the federal appeal board, the board of pension commissioners, the tribunal, and the appeal court, year after year. Finally the man who was entitled to pension died, and his widow obtained the pension. The Ouellette case is somewhat similar. It was a case in which the board of pension commissioners challenged the jurisdiction of the federal appeal board. When the federal appeal board was challenged these cases were left in the air. I wish also to support the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth in his observations with respect to the proceedings of the auditor general. I find in a report of the special committee on pensions and returned soldiers problems which sat in 1930 that the members of the committee, of which the minister was one and the Minister of Railways and Canals was another, protested vigorously against any assumption by t'he auditor general that he could act as a kind of appeal court from the board of pension commissioners. At that time it was brought to the notice of the committee by the returned soldiers' organizations, by Lieutenant Colonel Lafleche and others that the auditor general had been going into the department and to all intents and purposes had been reviewing cases. The reference is to be found at page 179 of the report. At that time the intervention had not gone very far, but considerable indignation 'had been expressed by members of the committee. I regret to learn that the auditor general has taken it upon himself again to intervene in matters of pensions. It was pointed out before this committee, as has been pointed out to-night in committee of the whole house, that the auditor general does not interfere with decisions of the exchequer court or of the supreme court, and he has no more right to interfere with decisions made by the board of pension commissioners. The board of pension commissioners were appointed to act independently of parliament in rendering decisions. They were to act independently of the minister, and were supposed to have the widest possible powers to deal with matters of pensions. I protest against the auditor general trying to arrogate to himself the power to overrule decisions of what, after all, is the competent court to deal with such matters.

As I read the statements of the Minister of Justice and the Prime Minister made some weeks ago-unfortunately I was not present in the house-I realize the difficulties referred to by the Minister of Justice. It may be that if the law is strictly interpreted, and the Department of Justice must do that, in many cases the decision will be against the pensioner, that is, that the marriages were not actually legal. I agree with the Minister of Justice that there are many cases where the marriages were not valid when considered according to the strict letter of the law, but in common decency and in common equity these cases should be treated [DOT] as though the marriages were valid. In many cases the parties thought they were married; they married in good faith. Sometimes a death was assumed or a divorce had been granted in another country which was not valid here. Legislation of some sort may be necessary in order to cover these points. While I am on my feet I should like to add my word to what has been said as to the jurisdiction assumed by the auditor general. But we found that the auditor general had constituted himself as a sort of appeal court to decide questions of entitlement, of diagnosis, as to whether a pension should have been granted or as to whether a disability was attributable. The committee resented this very keenly and I think the pension commissioners did also. It was our

understanding that in view of the strong expression of unanimous opinion, that practice would come to an end. I regret extremely that the practice still remains. As a matter of fact, I have had evidence that it still continues. I know of cases where pensions have been discontinued because such decisions have been made.
There is one other point with which I should like to deal, the policy of reductions in pensions. I wholly accept the minister's statement that it is not the policy of the government or of the department to reduce pensions. However, there is a firm conviction in the minds of a great many returned men, a conviction which I share after having perused many of the files and discussed many of the cases, that in many instances this is the policy of the pension commission. Two or three years ago whenever a pensioner appealed to me stating that his disability was increasing and his pension had become inadequate, I always made an effort to have a reboarding. I felt that as a result of a reboarding his pension would be increased, but during the past two or three years I have been very reluctant to advise a reboarding, no matter how obvious the case appeared to me. I doubt whether it needs to be amended, but I do think a little more sympathetic consideration and wider interpretation should be given in many cases. As the result of the general feeling in parliament and the almost unanimous expression of opinion by the convention of returned men held here not very long ago, I hope some changes will be made along these lines.

May I join with my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre in paying tribute to the manner in which the War Veterans' Allowance Act has been administered. I do so with perhaps greater pleasure in that personally I was one of those who, when this act was first introduced, did not believe it would work. I am pleased to admit that I had not a proper appreciation of how well a government board could function. The War Veterans' Allowance Act was introduced in 1930 by Doctor King, then Minister of Pensions and National Health, and I do not think any bill introduced during that session met such a storm of abuse and opposition. But strange as it may seem, it is perhaps the only piece of soldier legislation which has ever been put before this house during the past fifteen years that has been an unqualified success. The opposition of the day, and a great many on the government side, did not believe that the act could possibly operate properly. A good many of us did not believe in the principle of it. Before the committee objections were made against it. But, largely owing I think to the tact and ability it has shown and to the fact that it has been let severely alone, the board has received praise from all sides; I think there has hardly been a convention of the war veterans' associations or of the legion at which resolutions complimentary to this board have not been passed. I think we should say these things and give some credit to Doctor King on whose initiative the legislation was placed on our statutes. Doctor King was often severely criticized the same as the minister who is at present carrying on the affairs of the department; the opposition to his estimates was always very energetic, but I think it must be some consolation to him that he did put on the statute books one piece of legislation which is generally recognized as being sound.

It is a valuable lesson to have that where one wants a great many things done well one should do them and not go to a committee. Then in reference to this allowance, there is a point which has not been mentioned but which comes under my observation: an advantage in connection with the war veterans' allowances is that it results in a decrease in the number of cases that go to hospital. It gives a comfort to them, and they prefer staying at home.

I want to say a word regarding this act. I am expecting, and I think probably the minister is expecting, that it will not be long before the provisions of this act will have to be somewhat widened. The War Veteranss Allowance Act was designed to take the place of all the schemes and plans which had been put forward along the lines of soldiers' homes and care of soldiers and burnt out veterans, that is those suffering from something other than war disability, old soldiers whom the country did not want to see on the street. The principal provisions are, first, that any old soldier in need gets old age pension ten years earlier than other citizens; second, that a soldier who is permanently unemployable gets an allowance, and third, that one who is getting a small pension will have it supplemented. It is the provision as to "permanently unemployable" that seems to me may have to be extended before long. Whether a man is permanently unemployable depends of course on the judgment of medical men. But as they get older it seems to me the country will have to give much more attention to these men who have served overseas, who may not be suffering from war disability but whom the country wants to see taken care of. I would ask the minister and his officers to give consideration to the possibility of extending that provision, perhaps making it less rigorous as far as unemployability is concerned, with the idea of taking care of a greater number of men. It would be good business economically to do it; he will not have as many applying for hospital

care and meritorious or compassionate allowances if they are paid something from the treasury of the country and kept self-respecting.
I join with my hon. friends in what they have said in regard to the administration of the board. In my experience it has been uniformly good. That does not mean that all applications have been granted by any means, but that there has been sympathetic attitude and wisdom and soundness in the board's actions which has reflected credit on their administration and been most satisfactory to those interested in the problems of ex-service men.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I may say to the committee that what the hon. member for Shel-burne-Yarmouth has just referred to in regard to the care of men with chronic disabilities, old soldiers, is being developed, and has been in course of development for the last few years. It is getting on slowly, not in the way of building soldiers' homes just now, but the men are encouraged to come into hospitals and make their homes there on a certain financial arrangement. When that becomes a little more recognized and developed I think it will mean that in the future there will be soldiers' homes for many of the men.
